unit-alg-t2-05.title: Topic 2 · 2-5 Completing the Square
unit-alg-t2-05.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 2-5: Completing the Square

cards.def:
**Adding the right constant to x² + bx to turn it into a perfect square trinomial.**
• That constant is always (b/2)².
• It works for ANY quadratic equation, not just ones that happen to factor nicely.
cards.hint: Half the middle coefficient, then squared — that's the number you're always looking for.

cards.term: The constant that completes the square
cards.def:
**For x² + bx, add (b/2)² to make it a perfect square trinomial: x² + bx + (b/2)² = (x + b/2)².**
• Whatever you add to one side of an equation, you must add to the other side too.
• The result always factors as (x + b/2)² — a single squared binomial.
cards.hint: The number inside the resulting binomial is always half of b — nothing fancier.

cards.def:
**Move the constant to the other side, complete the square, then take the square root of both sides.**
• Once you have (x + p)² = q, taking the square root gives x + p = ±√q.
• If q is negative, the solutions come out complex — the method still works exactly the same way.
cards.hint: The ± only shows up once you take the square root — never before that step.

cards.def:
**If an equation is already a perfect square trinomial set equal to a number, skip straight to taking the square root of both sides.**
• This is the same idea as completing the square, just for an equation that's already done the hard part.
• Still remember the ± when you take the square root.
cards.hint: Recognize a perfect square trinomial and you can skip the "complete" step entirely.

cards.term: Completing the square with a leading coefficient
cards.def:
**Factor the leading coefficient out of the x² and x terms FIRST, then complete the square inside the parentheses.**
• y = ax² + bx + c becomes a(x² + (b/a)x) + c before completing the square.
• Whatever constant you add inside the parentheses gets multiplied by a before it affects the rest of the equation.
cards.hint: The (b/2)² step happens on the INSIDE coefficient, b/a — not on the original b.

cards.term: Writing a quadratic in vertex form
cards.def:
**Completing the square turns standard form directly into vertex form — it's the same process either way.**
• y = ax² + bx + c becomes y = a(x − h)² + k.
• This works for finding the vertex WITHOUT the h = −b/2a formula — the two methods always agree.
cards.hint: Completing the square and the h = −b/2a formula are two roads to the exact same vertex.

cards.term: Example: solving a perfect square trinomial equation
cards.def:
**64 = x² + 20x + 100 rewrites as 64 = (x + 10)², so x = −2 or x = −18.**
• Taking the square root: x + 10 = ±8.
• Two solutions come from the ± every time, unless the square root is exactly 0.
cards.hint: √64 = 8, and then it splits into two separate equations: x+10=8 and x+10=−8.

cards.term: Example: completing the square from scratch
cards.def:
**To solve x² + 10x + 7 = 0: move the 7, add 25 to both sides, and get (x + 5)² = 18.**
• x² + 10x = −7, then x² + 10x + 25 = −7 + 25 = 18.
• The solutions are x = −5 ± 3√2 — completing the square works even when the answer isn't a whole number.
cards.hint: Half of 10 is 5; 5 squared is 25 — that's the number added to both sides.

cards.term: Application: dimensions from area and perimeter
cards.def:
**A rectangle problem with known perimeter and area turns into a quadratic — completing the square solves for the missing side length.**
• Express one dimension in terms of the other using the perimeter.
• Substitute into the area formula, then complete the square to solve.
cards.hint: Perimeter gives you the relationship between the sides; area gives you the equation to solve.

questions.q: What number completes the square for x² + 12x?
questions.hint: Take half of the middle coefficient, then square it.
steps: The constant that completes the square is always (b/2)², where b is the coefficient of x.
Here b = 12, so half of it is 6.
6² = 36, so 36 is the number that completes the square.

ex.main: **36.** x² + 12x + 36 factors perfectly as (x + 6)².

questions.q: What number completes the square for x² − 18x?
questions.hint: Half of −18, then squared.
steps: Half of −18 is −9.
So 81 completes the square.

ex.main: **81.** x² − 18x + 81 factors as (x − 9)².

questions.q: What are the solutions of 64 = x² + 20x + 100?
questions.hint: The right side is already a perfect square trinomial — rewrite it as a squared binomial first.
steps: x² + 20x + 100 is a perfect square trinomial: it equals (x + 10)².
So the equation is 64 = (x + 10)².
Take the square root of both sides: x + 10 = ±8, giving x = −2 or x = −18.

questions.q: How can x² + 8x − 5 = 0 be rewritten in the form (x + p)² = q?
questions.hint: Move the constant first, then find and add the number that completes the square.
steps: Move the constant: x² + 8x = 5.
Find the number that completes the square: half of 8 is 4, and 4² = 16. Add 16 to both sides: x² + 8x + 16 = 5 + 16 = 21.
The left side factors as (x + 4)², so the equation is (x + 4)² = 21.

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² + 10x + 7 = 0?
questions.hint: Complete the square, then take the square root — the answer won't be a whole number here.
steps: Move the constant: x² + 10x = −7.
Complete the square: half of 10 is 5, 5² = 25. Add 25 to both sides: x² + 10x + 25 = −7 + 25 = 18, so (x + 5)² = 18.
Take the square root: x + 5 = ±√18 = ±3√2, so x = −5 ± 3√2.

ex.main: **x = −5 ± 3√2.** Completing the square works exactly the same way even when the final answer involves a square root instead of a whole number.

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² − 4x − 3 = 0?
questions.hint: Complete the square using half of −4.
steps: Move the constant: x² − 4x = 3.
Complete the square: half of −4 is −2, (−2)² = 4. Add 4 to both sides: x² − 4x + 4 = 3 + 4 = 7, so (x − 2)² = 7.
Take the square root: x − 2 = ±√7, so x = 2 ± √7.

questions.q: What are the solutions of 2x² + 8x − 24 = 0?
questions.hint: Divide out the leading coefficient before completing the square.
steps: Divide every term by 2: x² + 4x − 12 = 0.
Move the constant and complete the square: x² + 4x = 12, then add (4/2)² = 4: x² + 4x + 4 = 16, so (x + 2)² = 16.
Take the square root: x + 2 = ±4, so x = 2 or x = −6.

ex.main: **x = 2 and x = −6.** Dividing out the leading coefficient first turns this into an a = 1 problem, which is much easier to complete the square on.

questions.q: What is y = −3x² + 12x − 7 written in vertex form?
questions.hint: Factor out −3 from the x² and x terms first, then complete the square inside.
steps: Factor −3 out of the first two terms: y = −3(x² − 4x) − 7.
Complete the square inside the parentheses: half of −4 is −2, squared is 4. Add 4 inside — but since it's multiplied by −3, subtract −3(4) = −12 outside to balance: y = −3(x² − 4x + 4) − 7 + 12.
Simplify: y = −3(x − 2)² + 5.

ex.main: **y = −3(x − 2)² + 5.** The vertex is (2, 5) — completing the square finds it without ever using the h = −b/2a formula.

questions.q: What is the maximum or minimum value of y = 2x² − 8x + 3?
questions.hint: Complete the square to find the vertex, then check the sign of a to know maximum vs minimum.
steps: Factor out 2: y = 2(x² − 4x) + 3.
Complete the square inside: half of −4 is −2, squared is 4. y = 2(x² − 4x + 4) + 3 − 2(4) = 2(x − 2)² + 3 − 8 = 2(x − 2)² − 5.
a = 2 is positive, so this is a minimum, and the minimum value is −5, the vertex's y-coordinate.

ex.main: **Minimum of −5.**

questions.q: A farmer has 200 m of fencing for a rectangular pen and wants an area of 2,400 m². Using ℓ for length and completing the square, what are the possible dimensions?
questions.hint: Use the perimeter to write width in terms of length, then set up the area equation.
steps: From the perimeter: 2ℓ + 2w = 200, so w = 100 − ℓ.
Substitute into the area formula: ℓ(100 − ℓ) = 2400, which rearranges to ℓ² − 100ℓ + 2400 = 0.
Complete the square: ℓ² − 100ℓ + 2500 = −2400 + 2500, so (ℓ − 50)² = 100, giving ℓ = 50 ± 10, or ℓ = 60 or ℓ = 40. Either way, the dimensions are 40 m by 60 m.

ex.main: **40 m by 60 m.** Completing the square solves the quadratic; checking both solutions against the original perimeter confirms they describe the same rectangle from two directions.

questions.q: After completing the square, an equation is in the form (x − 3)² = −9. What does this tell you about the solutions?
opts: The solutions are complex, since you'd need to take the square root of a negative number
The equation has no solutions of any kind
The solutions are x = 3 and x = −9
There was an arithmetic error, since this can never happen
questions.hint: What happens when you take the square root of a negative number?
steps: Taking the square root of both sides gives x − 3 = ±√−9.
√−9 is not a real number — it simplifies to 3i using the imaginary unit.
So the solutions exist, but they're complex: x = 3 ± 3i, not real numbers.

ex.main: **The solutions are complex.** A negative number under the square root is not an error — completing the square works perfectly well on equations with complex solutions.

questions.q: Khalan says only quadratic equations with a leading coefficient of 1 can be solved by completing the square. Is Khalan correct?
opts: No — dividing (or factoring out) the leading coefficient first lets any quadratic be solved this way
Yes, completing the square only works when a = 1
No — completing the square only works when a is negative
Yes, but only if b is also 1
questions.hint: Think about what the first step is when a isn't 1.
steps: When a ≠ 1, the first step is to divide every term by a (or factor a out), which turns the leading coefficient into 1.
After that step, completing the square proceeds exactly the same way as when a was already 1.
So Khalan is incorrect — every quadratic equation can be solved by completing the square, regardless of its leading coefficient.

ex.main: **No.** Dividing out (or factoring out) the leading coefficient first is the one extra step that makes any quadratic ready for completing the square.

questions.q: What is the first step in solving x² + 6x = 59 by completing the square?
opts: Find (6/2)² = 9 and add it to both sides
Factor the left side as it stands
Take the square root of both sides immediately
questions.hint: The equation is already set up with the constant moved — what's the very next move?
steps: The constant is already isolated on the right side, so the next step is finding the number that completes the square.
That number is (b/2)² = (6/2)² = 9.
Add 9 to both sides: x² + 6x + 9 = 59 + 9, giving (x + 3)² = 68.

ex.main: **Find (6/2)² = 9 and add it to both sides.** You can't take a meaningful square root until the left side is actually a perfect square trinomial.

questions.q: A student completing the square on x² − 14x + 5 = 0 adds 49 to only the LEFT side of the equation. What is their error?
opts: Whatever is added to one side must also be added to the other side to keep the equation balanced
49 is the wrong number — it should be 7
The student should have subtracted 49 instead of adding it
There is no error — the equation is still correct
questions.hint: Think about what keeps an equation true when you change one side of it.
steps: Completing the square requires adding (b/2)² to BOTH sides of the equation, not just one.
Here, half of −14 is −7, and (−7)² = 49 — that part is correct.
But adding 49 only to the left side breaks the equality; it must be added to the right side too: x² − 14x + 49 = −5 + 49.

ex.main: **Whatever is added to one side must also be added to the other.** This is the same balance rule as any equation — completing the square doesn't get an exception.

questions.q: What is x² + 14x + 49 in factored (squared binomial) form?
questions.hint: Take the square root of the constant term to find the number inside the binomial.
steps: Check: is 49 the square of half of 14? Half of 14 is 7, and 7² = 49 — yes.
So x² + 14x + 49 is a perfect square trinomial.
It factors as (x + 7)².

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² + 2x + 1 = 25?
questions.hint: The left side is already a perfect square trinomial.
steps: Recognize x² + 2x + 1 as (x + 1)², since half of 2 is 1 and 1² = 1.
So the equation is (x + 1)² = 25.
Take the square root: x + 1 = ±5, so x = 4 or x = −6.

questions.q: A picture frame problem leads to the equation w² + 6w − 40 = 0, where w is the frame's width in inches. What is the width?
questions.hint: Complete the square to solve, then throw out any solution that can't be a real width.
steps: Move the constant and complete the square: w² + 6w = 40, then add (6/2)² = 9: w² + 6w + 9 = 49, so (w + 3)² = 49.
Take the square root: w + 3 = ±7, so w = 4 or w = −10.
A width can't be negative, so w = −10 is rejected. The width is 4 inches.

ex.main: **4 inches.** Completing the square hands you two solutions; the physical context — a width can't be negative — is what picks the real one.

questions.q: To complete the square for x² − 5x, what constant should be added?
questions.hint: Half of −5 is a fraction — square it carefully.
steps: Half of −5 is −5/2.
So 25/4 is the constant that completes the square.

ex.main: **25/4.** The method doesn't change just because b is odd — the answer is simply a fraction this time.

questions.q: What is y = x² + 6x − 6 written in vertex form?
questions.hint: Complete the square on x² + 6x, then adjust the constant.
steps: Half of 6 is 3, and 3² = 9. Add and subtract 9: y = x² + 6x + 9 − 9 − 6.
The first three terms form a perfect square: y = (x + 3)² − 9 − 6.
Combine the constants: y = (x + 3)² − 15.

questions.q: What are the solutions of 7x² + 56x − 22 = 0, rounded to the nearest hundredth?
questions.hint: Divide by 7 first, then complete the square — this one won't come out to whole numbers.
steps: Divide every term by 7: x² + 8x − 22/7 = 0, so x² + 8x = 22/7.
Complete the square: half of 8 is 4, squared is 16. x² + 8x + 16 = 22/7 + 16 ≈ 19.14, so (x + 4)² ≈ 19.14.
Take the square root: x + 4 ≈ ±4.38, so x ≈ 0.38 or x ≈ −8.38.

ex.main: **x ≈ 0.38 and x ≈ −8.38.** Not every equation completes the square into nice whole numbers — the method still works, it just needs a calculator for the last step.
